p: Two of the three critical editions, with the Byzantine text, begin Martha's words with "But." The SBLGNT leaves it out.

readings.w: NA28 (in square brackets), Tyndale House, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "But I know, that even now")
SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

why: The Plain follows NA28 and the Tyndale House edition here against the SBLGNT. The word is small but it shapes Martha's tone: "But even now" turns from her reproach (11:21) to hope. The manuscripts are divided, as the square brackets in NA27 and NA28 show; see the NA28 apparatus for the witnesses.
b: A similar small difference is at 12:9, where NA28, Tyndale House and Westcott-Hort have "the great crowd" with the article and the SBLGNT "a great crowd" without it. The Plain's "A great crowd" follows the SBLGNT; the meaning is the same.

p: A few early witnesses have Jesus say only "I am the resurrection."

readings.w: Nearly all Greek manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s) and Papyrus 66 (about 200); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine, Textus Receptus (KJV)
Papyrus 45 (200s, as far as it can be read), one Old Latin manuscript, the Sinaitic Syriac (300s–400s) and Cyprian (mid-200s), as reported by Metzger

why: The longer reading has overwhelming support. The words may have been dropped because Martha had spoken only of the resurrection (11:24), so "and the life" looked like an extra.
b: Some modern versions mention the shorter reading in a footnote. The saying's two promises in 11:25b–26, "will live" and "will never die," match the two words "resurrection" and "life," which favors the longer text.

p: The KJV has the mourners say, "She is going to the tomb." The older text says they thought so.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75 (about 200), Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s); SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
Codex Alexandrinus (400s), Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "saying, She goeth unto the grave")

why: "Supposing" has the older and wider support. "Saying" is a common, easy word that could replace a less expected one.

p: Later manuscripts and the KJV add that the stone was taken from where the dead man lay.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
readings.en: So they took away the stone.

readings.w: Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "from the place where the dead was laid")
readings.orig: ἦραν οὖν τὸν λίθον οὗ ἦν ὁ τεθνηκὼς κείμενος
readings.en: So they took away the stone from where the dead man was lying.
readings.plain: They moved the stone away from the place where the dead man was lying.

why: The added words are missing from the oldest manuscripts and look like an explanation. Copyists also differed on exactly how to word it, a common sign of an addition.

p: Caiaphas says it is good "for you"; the KJV reads "for us."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the editions' choice; the full list of manuscripts is in the NA28 apparatus)
Byzantine majority text, Textus Receptus (KJV "it is expedient for us")

why: All the critical editions read "you," which fits Caiaphas' scornful tone ("You don't know anything"). In later Greek the two words sounded alike, so copyists often confused them.

a: the man Jesus had raised from the dead
p: The KJV says Lazarus "had been dead," whom "he raised." The older text is shorter.

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
readings.en: whom Jesus raised from the dead
readings.plain: the man Jesus had raised from the dead

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "which had been dead, whom he raised from the dead")
readings.orig: ὁ τεθνηκώς, ὃν ἤγειρεν ἐκ νεκρῶν
readings.en: who had died, whom he raised from the dead
readings.plain: the man who had died, whom he had raised from the dead

why: The shorter text is older. "Who had died" repeats what the reader knows and was probably added from 11:39 and 11:44.

p: Later manuscripts and the KJV call him "Judas Iscariot, Simon's son," as John does in 6:71 and 13:2.

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Judas Iscariot, Simon's son")

why: The father's name is probably borrowed from 6:71 and 13:2, where it is secure. The Byzantine text also changes the word order of the verse.

a: , so that she can keep it
t: "So that she may keep" or "she has kept"?
p: The oldest text has a puzzling "so that she may keep it." Later copies, and the KJV, smooth it to "she has kept this."

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Bezae; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
readings.en: so that she may keep it
readings.plain: , so that she can keep it

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "against the day of my burying hath she kept this")

why: The harder reading is older and better supported. Copyists who wondered how Mary could "keep" what she had just poured out changed it to "she has kept," which Metzger calls a clear attempt to ease the difficulty. See the note on this verse for what the older wording means.

a: For you always have poor people among you, but you do not always have me.
t: A verse missing from two witnesses
p: Codex Bezae and the Sinaitic Syriac lack this verse. All other witnesses have it.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, and almost all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Byzantine, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: τοὺς πτωχοὺς γὰρ πάντοτε ἔχετε μεθ᾽ ἑαυτῶν, ἐμὲ δὲ οὐ πάντοτε ἔχετε
readings.en: For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me
readings.plain: For you always have poor people among you, but you do not always have me.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (400s) and the Sinaitic Syriac, as reported by Metzger

why: The verse is in the great early codices and nearly every manuscript. Its absence from two witnesses is probably an accident or a dropping of words that some thought were borrowed from Mark 14:7 and Matthew 26:11.

a: the crowd that was with him when he summoned
p: One Greek letter changes what the crowd testifies: some manuscripts say the crowd told "that" he raised Lazarus.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, Byzantine majority; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.plain: the crowd that was with him when he summoned

readings.w: Papyrus 66, Codex Bezae, and some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses, as reported by Metzger
readings.plain: the crowd that was with him, that he had summoned

why: "When" (hote) has the broader support. With "that" (hoti), two crowds become one, and 12:18 reads less smoothly; most editors think the change came by accident, since the words differ by one letter.

p: The older text puts the loss in the present; the KJV, with later manuscripts, makes it future.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles (the editions' choice; see the NA28 apparatus for the manuscripts)
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "shall lose it")

why: All the critical editions read the present. The future matches the parallels in Matthew and Luke and the future "will guard" later in this verse, so copyists likely changed it to match.

p: Some manuscripts have Jesus pray "glorify your Son." Codex Bezae adds "with the glory I had with you."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, Byzantine majority; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Textus Receptus (KJV)
Codex Regius (L, 700s), family 1, family 13 and a few others, as reported by Metzger
Codex Bezae (400s), adding words drawn from 17:5, as reported by Metzger
readings.orig: δόξασόν σου τὸ ὄνομα + words from 17:5
readings.en: glorify your name with the glory I had with you before the world existed
readings.plain: your name with the glory I had with you before the world existed

why: "Your name" is supported by the oldest and most varied witnesses. "Your Son" comes from 17:1, and Bezae's long reading from 17:5.

p: A few important early witnesses say Jesus will draw "all things" to himself, and the Latin Vulgate follows them.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, Byzantine majority; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Textus Receptus (KJV "all men")
Papyrus 66 (about 200), Codex Sinaiticus as first written, Codex Bezae, Old Latin and the Latin Vulgate (omnia)

why: "Everyone" has strong and varied support and fits the context of the Greeks who want to see Jesus (12:20–21). "All things" may have arisen from the similar look of the two words or from a wish to give the saying a cosmic scope (compare Colossians 1:20).
b: Because the Vulgate reads omnia, "all things," Western readers had to explain it. Augustine took it to mean all kinds of people, or the whole of a person (Tractates on John 52.11).

p: The KJV reads "when he saw his glory." The older text says "because."

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
Codex Bezae, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "when he saw his glory")

why: "Because" is the older reading. "When" is easier, since it simply dates Isaiah's words to his vision; it differs by one letter.
b: A few witnesses also read "the glory of his God" or "the glory of God," which avoids saying Isaiah saw Christ's glory. No modern edition follows them.

p: The KJV says "believe not." The older manuscripts say "does not keep" Jesus' sayings.

readings.w: Papyrus 66 and 75, Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "and believe not")

why: "Keep" has the older and wider support. "Believe" fits the many uses of that verb in 12:44–46 and probably came in from them.
